subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Sweet Cake Adventure
hook: Two friends divide a birthday cake and discover the magic of fractions.

slides.title: The Birthday Cake Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother baked a big round cake. She asked Anaya and Ravi to divide it fairly among their 4 friends. Anaya cut the cake into 4 equal pieces.

points.label: Setup
points.text: One whole cake divided into 4 equal parts

slides.inSimpleWords: One cake cut into 4 equal pieces makes fractions.

image.alt: The Birthday Cake Puzzle — Fractions

slides.title: Understanding Numerator and Denominator
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at one slice. 'That's 1 out of 4 pieces,' he said. Anaya wrote: 1/4.

points.label: Numerator
points.text: The number on top (1) = how many pieces we take

points.label: Denominator
points.text: The number below (4) = total equal pieces

points.label: Fraction
points.text: 1/4 means one part out of four

slides.inSimpleWords: Top number = pieces taken. Bottom number = total pieces.

image.alt: Understanding Numerator and Denominator — Fractions

slides.title: Working with Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya took 2 slices for herself and Ravi. That was 2/4 of the cake.

example.problem: If Anaya eats 2 slices out of 4, what fraction is that?
example.solution: 2 slices taken ÷ 4 total slices = 2/4 (which simplifies to 1/2)

points.label: Remember
points.text: Multiple parts of the same fraction add together

slides.inSimpleWords: Two slices out of four is 2/4 or half the cake.

image.alt: Working with Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mother cut another identical cake into 8 pieces. Ravi took 4 slices from this cake. 'Look, Anaya! I have the same amount as you!' he said.

points.label: Same Amount
points.text: 2/4 from first cake = 4/8 from second cake

slides.inSimpleWords: Half a cake = 2/4 = 4/8. Different numbers, same part.

image.alt: Equivalent Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: At the party, Anaya's friend got 1/2 of a chocolate bar, and another friend got 2/4 of an identical bar. 'They're the same!' said Ravi.

example.problem: Which is bigger: 1/2 or 2/4?
example.solution: 1/2 = 2/4. They are equal; neither is bigger.

points.label: Tip
points.text: Draw or fold paper to see equivalent fractions

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount, just different names.

image.alt: Comparing Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Your Fraction Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya has a ribbon 1 meter long. She cuts it into 5 equal pieces for her hair clips. Ravi asks: 'What fraction is each piece?'

points.label: Think
points.text: If 1 ribbon is cut into 5 equal pieces, each piece is __/5

slides.inSimpleWords: One ribbon, five equal pieces: each piece is 1/5.

image.alt: Your Fraction Challenge — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions in Daily Life
slides.storyContext: Anaya realized fractions are everywhere: half a glass of milk, one-third of the journey completed, two-quarter hours at school.
slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions help us describe parts of things in real life.

image.alt: Fractions in Daily Life — Fractions

slides.title: Adding Simple Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi ate 1/4 of a pizza. Anaya ate 2/4 of the same pizza. Together, how much did they eat?

example.solution: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4 (add numerators, keep denominator same)

points.label: Rule
points.text: Same denominator? Add top numbers only.

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/4 plus 2/4 equals 3/4 of the pizza.

image.alt: Adding Simple Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Proper and Improper Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya's bakery sold cakes in pieces. If someone bought 5 pieces when each whole cake had 4 pieces, that's 5/4 (more than one whole cake!).

points.label: Improper Fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ Denominator (more than or equal to 1 whole)

slides.inSimpleWords: 5/4 is bigger than one whole cake piece.

image.alt: Proper and Improper Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that fractions are parts of wholes, written with numerator and denominator, and found everywhere from cakes to ribbons to journeys.
slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions name parts of a whole using two numbers.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson — Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Ravi and Anaya's Compass Adventure
hook: Two friends use a spinning compass to discover how turns create angles.

slides.title: The Spinning Compass Game
slides.storyContext: Ravi found a toy compass on the beach. Anaya asked him to spin it slowly. 'When it completes one full turn, that's a complete angle,' she explained, pointing at how the needle went all the way around.
slides.inSimpleWords: One full spin around is called 360 degrees.

image.alt: The Spinning Compass Game — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Understanding Right Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya held the compass steady and told Ravi to spin it just one-quarter of the way. 'Stop!' she said. The needle had turned 90 degrees. 'That's a right angle,' Anaya smiled, 'like the corner of our classroom door.'

points.label: Symbol
points.text: A small square in the corner marks a right angle

slides.inSimpleWords: 90 degrees is one-quarter turn, like a door corner.

image.alt: Understanding Right Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Measuring Angles with Turns
slides.storyContext: Ravi turned the compass halfway around. Anaya counted: '180 degrees! That's a straight line, Ravi.' They realized half a turn makes a straight angle.

example.problem: If Ravi spins the compass halfway, how many degrees has he turned?
example.solution: Half a turn = 180 degrees (straight line)

slides.inSimpleWords: Halfway around is 180 degrees, making a straight line.

image.alt: Measuring Angles with Turns — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Acute, Right, and Obtuse Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya taught Ravi three types of angles using her arms. A small hug (arms close) = acute angle (less than 90°). Arms at a corner = right angle (90°). A big hug (arms wide) = obtuse angle (more than 90° but less than 180°).

points.label: Obtuse
points.text: More than 90 but less than 180 degrees (wide)

slides.inSimpleWords: Three angle types: small, corner, or wide hug.

image.alt: Acute, Right, and Obtuse Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Finding Angles in Your Classroom
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya walked around their school. They found a right angle where the wall meets the floor (90°), an acute angle at the roof peak, and an obtuse angle at the open window.

example.problem: The window opens 120 degrees. Is this acute, right, or obtuse?
example.solution: 120° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it's obtuse.

slides.inSimpleWords: 120 degrees is wider than a corner, so it's obtuse.

image.alt: Finding Angles in Your Classroom — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool
slides.storyContext: Anaya pulled out a protractor. 'This tool measures angles!' she said. She placed it on the compass where the needle pointed and read the number: 45 degrees. Ravi marveled: 'That's exactly one-eighth of a full turn!'

points.label: How to Use
points.text: Center at the angle point, align one ray at 0

slides.inSimpleWords: A protractor measures angles using its numbered semicircle.

image.alt: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Estimate the Angle
slides.storyContext: Ravi opened the door slowly and asked Anaya to guess the angle without measuring. The door was open about a quarter way. 'About 90 degrees?' guessed Anaya. Ravi smiled: 'Close! It's actually 85 degrees.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Try guessing angles before you measure them.

image.alt: Estimate the Angle — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Clock Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya noticed the school clock. 'The hour hand and minute hand make angles!' She calculated: at 3 o'clock, the hands make a 90-degree angle. At 6 o'clock, they make 180 degrees.

example.problem: At 3:00, what angle do the clock hands make?
example.solution: Hour hand at 3, minute hand at 12 = 90 degrees (right angle)

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make angles that change every minute.

image.alt: Clock Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Angles in Nature and Design
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at the river flowing and Anaya at the trees. 'Branches make angles!' said Ravi. 'So do river bends,' added Anaya. They realized angles were everywhere: bird wings, roofs, ladders, and even the way people sit.
slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are found in nature, buildings, and our bodies.

image.alt: Angles in Nature and Design — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Discovery
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that angles measure turns, come in different sizes (acute, right, obtuse), and are measured in degrees using a protractor. They're everywhere!

points.label: All Around
points.text: Angles in nature, buildings, clocks, and more

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles measure turns and are found everywhere we look.

image.alt: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Discovery — Angles as Turns

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Treasure Map Journey
hook: Two friends use distance to find a hidden treasure across their village.

slides.title: The Mystery Map
slides.storyContext: Anaya's grandmother gave them an old map showing a treasure buried 'far from the village well.' But how far is 'far'? Anaya decided they needed to measure. She marked the well as the starting point and began measuring the distance using a measuring tape.
slides.inSimpleWords: Distance measures how far apart two places are.

image.alt: The Mystery Map — Far and Near

slides.title: Units of Measurement
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked: 'How do we measure distance?' Anaya showed him different tools: her handspan (short), a meter stick (1 meter), and a measuring wheel (for long distances). 'We use different units depending on what we're measuring,' she explained.

points.label: Meter (m)
points.text: For medium things like rooms or trees

points.label: Kilometer (km)
points.text: For long distances like between villages

slides.inSimpleWords: Use small units for near things, big units for far things.

image.alt: Units of Measurement — Far and Near

slides.title: Converting Units
slides.storyContext: Anaya measured a path and found it was 500 meters long. 'That's half a kilometer!' she said happily. Ravi wrote down the conversion: 100 cm = 1 meter, and 1000 meters = 1 kilometer.

example.problem: If the path to the treasure is 2 kilometers, how many meters is that?
example.solution: 2 km × 1000 = 2000 meters

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 kilometers is 2000 meters long.

image.alt: Converting Units — Far and Near

slides.title: Measuring Real Distances
slides.storyContext: Ravi stepped out and started walking while Anaya marked points on the map. 'One step is about half a meter,' Ravi called back. By counting steps, they estimated long distances without stopping.

points.label: Body Measures
points.text: Hand span, arm length, step length

slides.inSimpleWords: Our body can help estimate distances quickly.

image.alt: Measuring Real Distances — Far and Near

slides.title: Finding the Treasure Distance
slides.storyContext: Using the map scale (1 cm on map = 10 meters real distance), Anaya measured from the well to the marked treasure spot. The map distance was 5 cm. She calculated the real distance: 5 × 10 = 50 meters.

example.problem: Map scale: 1 cm = 20 meters. Treasure is 3 cm away on map. Real distance?
example.solution: 3 cm × 20 = 60 meters (real distance)

points.label: Map Scale
points.text: Always check the scale before trusting a map

slides.inSimpleWords: Map scale helps find real distances from drawn maps.

image.alt: Finding the Treasure Distance — Far and Near

slides.title: Your Distance Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya asks Ravi: 'The village market is 3 kilometers away. How many steps would you need to walk there if your step is half a meter?' Ravi started counting on his fingers!
slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate how many steps for a 3 kilometer walk.

image.alt: Your Distance Challenge — Far and Near

slides.title: Comparing Distances
slides.storyContext: At the market, Anaya and Ravi saw signs: 'School: 2 km away' and 'River: 1500 meters away.' 'The river is nearer!' Ravi realized. '1500 meters is only 1.5 kilometers, and 1.5 < 2,' explained Anaya.

points.label: Compare
points.text: Convert to same unit before comparing

slides.inSimpleWords: First change to the same unit, then compare distances.

image.alt: Comparing Distances — Far and Near

slides.title: Perimeter: Distance Around
slides.storyContext: Anaya drew a square field on her map (each side 100 meters). Ravi asked, 'How far around the whole field?' Anaya calculated: 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 400 meters. 'That's the perimeter!' she declared.

example.problem: A rectangular garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. What's the distance around it?
example.solution: Perimeter = 2 × (8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = 26 meters

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Distance all the way around a shape

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the total distance around a shape.

image.alt: Perimeter: Distance Around — Far and Near

slides.title: Distance in Time and Speed
slides.storyContext: When they finally walked to the treasure location, Ravi checked his watch: 30 minutes for 500 meters. 'We were walking at a certain speed,' Anaya said. 'Distance ÷ Time = Speed!'

points.label: Units
points.text: Meters per minute or kilometers per hour

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed tells us how far we travel in a certain time.

image.alt: Distance in Time and Speed — Far and Near

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Treasure Discovery
slides.storyContext: They found the treasure and realized distance shapes our world: maps, journeys, measurements, and speeds all depend on understanding far and near.

points.label: Units
points.text: cm, m, km for different distances

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is how far apart things are and how we measure.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Treasure Discovery — Far and Near

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Dairy Adventure
hook: Two friends help a farmer divide milk and count costs at a dairy farm.

slides.title: Welcome to the Dairy Farm
slides.storyContext: Anaya's uncle owns a dairy farm with 24 cows. He asked the children to help organize the milk bottles into crates. Anaya asked: 'How many bottles fit in each crate if we want them divided equally?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing things equally helps us share fairly.

image.alt: Welcome to the Dairy Farm — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Division: Sharing Equally
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya packed bottles into 6 crates: 4 in the first, 4 in the second, 4 in the third... 'Each crate has 4 bottles! That's fair,' Anaya realized. '24 ÷ 6 = 4,' she wrote.
slides.inSimpleWords: Division splits things fairly into equal groups.

image.alt: Division: Sharing Equally — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Division with Remainders
slides.storyContext: The next day, 28 liters of milk arrived, and Anaya wanted to fill bottles that hold 5 liters each. 'How many full bottles, and any milk left over?' asked Ravi. They calculated: 28 ÷ 5 = 5 full bottles with 3 liters remaining.

example.problem: Divide 28 liters into 5-liter bottles. How many full bottles and remainder?
example.solution: 28 ÷ 5 = 5 remainder 3 (5 full bottles, 3 liters left)

points.label: Remainder
points.text: The amount left after equal division

slides.inSimpleWords: 28 ÷ 5 makes 5 full bottles with 3 liters extra.

image.alt: Division with Remainders — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Multiplication and Division: Opposites
slides.storyContext: Anaya showed Ravi a clever trick. 'If 6 crates × 4 bottles = 24 bottles, then 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Multiplication and division undo each other!' She wrote: 6 × 4 = 24 AND 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

points.label: Check Division
points.text: Multiply quotient by divisor to verify

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply to combine groups; divide to separate groups.

image.alt: Multiplication and Division: Opposites — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Calculating Costs at the Dairy
slides.storyContext: Each bottle of milk costs 30 rupees. The farm sold 15 bottles. Ravi calculated: 15 × 30 = 450 rupees. But when a customer returned 5 bottles for a refund, Anaya divided: 450 ÷ 3 = 150 rupees (5 × 30).

example.problem: If milk is 30 rupees per bottle, how much for 8 bottles?
example.solution: 8 × 30 = 240 rupees

points.label: Repeated Addition
points.text: Multiplication is quicker than adding many times

slides.inSimpleWords: 8 bottles at 30 rupees each costs 240 rupees.

image.alt: Calculating Costs at the Dairy — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Your Farm Math Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya's uncle has 72 square meters of pasture land. He wants to divide it equally among his 8 cows for grazing. How much space does each cow get? (Hint: Use division!)
slides.inSimpleWords: Divide 72 by 8 to find space for each cow.

image.alt: Your Farm Math Challenge — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Grouping and Counting in Rows and Columns
slides.storyContext: Anaya arranged milk bottles on a shelf in 3 rows and 4 columns. 'That's 3 × 4 = 12 bottles total,' she said. Ravi rearranged them into 2 rows and 6 columns. 'Still 2 × 6 = 12 bottles, same amount, different shape!'

points.label: Array
points.text: Bottles arranged in rows and columns

slides.inSimpleWords: Rows times columns give the total, even if arranged differently.

image.alt: Grouping and Counting in Rows and Columns — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Word Problems from the Farm
slides.storyContext: The dairy worker has 36 bottle crates. He packs them into boxes that hold 9 crates each. Ravi questions: 'How many boxes does he need?' Anaya responds: '36 ÷ 9 = 4 boxes.'

example.problem: 36 crates ÷ 9 crates per box = ? boxes
example.solution: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 boxes needed

slides.inSimpleWords: 36 crates divide evenly into 4 boxes of 9 each.

image.alt: Word Problems from the Farm — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Division Patterns and Times Tables
slides.storyContext: Anaya noticed patterns in the dairy: '6 × 5 = 30, so 30 ÷ 5 = 6. When we know times tables, division is easy!' They practiced: 7 × 8 = 56, so 56 ÷ 8 = 7.

points.label: Pattern
points.text: If a × b = c, then c ÷ b = a

slides.inSimpleWords: Knowing multiplication helps us divide faster.

image.alt: Division Patterns and Times Tables — The Dairy Farm

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Dairy Farm Lessons
slides.storyContext: The children learned that division shares things fairly, multiplication and division are opposites, and both help us solve real problems on the farm.

points.label: Real Use
points.text: Farm costs, bottles, groups, and sharing

slides.inSimpleWords: Division and multiplication solve real farm problems.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Dairy Farm Lessons — The Dairy Farm

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Pattern Discovery
hook: Two friends find shapes and patterns everywhere in their town.

slides.title: Shapes in the Market
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi visited the village market. Anaya pointed: 'Look at all the shapes! Round tomatoes, square baskets, rectangular boxes!' Ravi replied, 'I see patterns too — the baskets are stacked in rows and columns.'

points.label: Observation
points.text: Shapes and patterns surround us daily

slides.inSimpleWords: Our world is full of shapes arranged in patterns.

image.alt: Shapes in the Market — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: 2D Shapes: Flat and Drawn
slides.storyContext: Anaya drew shapes on the ground with a stick. 'Triangle has 3 sides, square has 4 equal sides, circle has no corners, and rectangle has 4 sides but not all equal,' she explained, drawing each one.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: 4 sides, opposite sides equal, 4 right angles

points.label: Circle
points.text: No sides, no corners, perfectly round

slides.inSimpleWords: 2D shapes are flat with sides and corners.

image.alt: 2D Shapes: Flat and Drawn — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Finding Perimeter of Shapes
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked Anaya to find the distance around a triangular vegetable patch. One side was 5 meters, the second was 4 meters, and the third was 6 meters. Anaya added: 5 + 4 + 6 = 15 meters (perimeter).

example.problem: Triangle sides: 5 m, 4 m, 6 m. What's the perimeter?
example.solution: 5 + 4 + 6 = 15 meters

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Add all sides to get the distance around

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the total distance around any shape.

image.alt: Finding Perimeter of Shapes — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: 3D Shapes: Solid and Real
slides.storyContext: Ravi picked up an apple (sphere), a gift box (cube), and a carrot (cone). 'These are 3D shapes! They have length, width, and height. We can hold them!' Anaya listed more: cylinder (water pipe), pyramid (temple roof), and cuboid (brick).

points.label: Cylinder
points.text: Tube shape, circular tops and bottom

points.label: Pyramid
points.text: Pointed, triangular faces meeting at apex

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D shapes are solid and take up real space.

image.alt: 3D Shapes: Solid and Real — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Nets: Unfolding 3D Shapes
slides.storyContext: Anaya unfolded a cardboard box to show Ravi the net. 'If we unfold this cube, we get 6 squares! Folding them back makes the box again,' she demonstrated carefully.

example.problem: A cube's net shows 6 square faces. When folded, what shape forms?
example.solution: A cube (all 6 faces form a closed 3D shape)

points.label: Net
points.text: Flat unfolded version of a 3D shape

slides.inSimpleWords: Nets are flat patterns that fold into solid shapes.

image.alt: Nets: Unfolding 3D Shapes — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Patterns and Sequences
slides.storyContext: On the temple wall, Anaya found a repeating pattern: square, circle, triangle, square, circle, triangle... 'It repeats every 3 shapes!' said Ravi. They also noticed number patterns: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (adding 2 each time).

points.label: Repeating Pattern
points.text: Core unit repeats (shape, color, or number)

points.label: Growing Pattern
points.text: Each element increases by a fixed amount

points.label: Rule
points.text: The pattern follows a clear rule

slides.inSimpleWords: Patterns repeat or grow following a rule.

image.alt: Patterns and Sequences — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Identifying Pattern Rules
slides.storyContext: Anaya wrote: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. 'The pattern adds 3 each time,' said Ravi. 'Or multiplies by 3 from the position! First: 1×3, Second: 2×3, Third: 3×3,' said Anaya.

example.problem: Pattern: 3, 6, 9, 12, ?, ?. What are the next two numbers?
example.solution: 15, 18 (add 3 to each number)

slides.inSimpleWords: Pattern: 3, 6, 9... continues by adding 3 each time.

image.alt: Identifying Pattern Rules — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Your Pattern Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws a pattern on the ground: red circle, blue square, red circle, blue square... What comes next? And if the pattern starts again, how many shapes until we see two red circles in a row?

points.label: Think
points.text: Identify the rule, predict the next shape, count carefully

slides.inSimpleWords: Figure out pattern rules and predict what comes next.

image.alt: Your Pattern Challenge — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Symmetry and Reflection
slides.storyContext: Anaya folded a sheet of paper and drew a butterfly outline. When she unfolded it, a perfect butterfly appeared. 'It's symmetrical! Both sides are identical mirror images,' she exclaimed. Ravi found symmetry in a folded square and a circle.

points.label: Line of Symmetry
points.text: An imaginary line where we fold for two equal halves

points.label: Symmetrical
points.text: Both sides are identical mirror images

points.label: Examples
points.text: Butterfly wings, temple doors, flower petals

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetrical shapes have two identical mirrored halves.

image.alt: Symmetry and Reflection — Shapes and Patterns

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Shape and Pattern Journey
slides.storyContext: They learned that shapes (2D and 3D) are everywhere, patterns repeat or grow by rules, and symmetry creates beauty in nature and design.
slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes, patterns, and symmetry shape our beautiful world.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Shape and Pattern Journey — Shapes and Patterns

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Kitchen Experiment
hook: Two friends discover how to measure weight and capacity at home.

characters.name: Anaya
characters.role: chef in training who measures ingredients

slides.title: Baking a Cake with Math
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother was baking a cake and asked the children to weigh flour and measure milk. Anaya found the kitchen scale and milk measuring cup. 'So weight measures how heavy, and capacity measures how much liquid fits!' she realized.

points.label: Capacity
points.text: How much a container can hold

slides.inSimpleWords: Weight and capacity help us cook recipes correctly.

image.alt: Baking a Cake with Math — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Units of Weight
slides.storyContext: Ravi placed flour on the scale. 'It says 250 grams,' he read aloud. Anaya pointed to a bag of rice: '2 kilograms. That's much heavier!' She explained: 1000 grams = 1 kilogram.

points.label: Gram (g)
points.text: Small unit for light things (pencil, coins)

points.label: Kilogram (kg)
points.text: Larger unit for heavier things (people, bags)

slides.inSimpleWords: Grams for light things, kilograms for heavy things.

image.alt: Units of Weight — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Weighing Recipe Ingredients
slides.storyContext: The cake recipe needed: 200g flour, 100g sugar, 50g butter, and 200ml milk. Ravi weighed each. 'Total weight of dry ingredients: 200 + 100 + 50 = 350 grams!' he calculated.

example.problem: Recipe needs 200g flour + 100g sugar + 50g butter. Total dry weight?

points.label: Remember
points.text: Add weights carefully using the same unit

slides.inSimpleWords: Total ingredients: 200 + 100 + 50 = 350 grams.

image.alt: Weighing Recipe Ingredients — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Units of Capacity (Volume)
slides.storyContext: Anaya poured milk into a measuring cup marked with milliliters (ml). 'This measures how much liquid,' she said. She filled it to 250ml. Ravi asked about liters. 'One liter bottle holds 1000 milliliters!'

points.label: Milliliter (ml)
points.text: Small unit for small amounts of liquid

slides.inSimpleWords: Milliliters measure small amounts, liters measure big amounts.

image.alt: Units of Capacity (Volume) — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Converting and Comparing Capacities
slides.storyContext: Anaya had a 2-liter bottle of juice and a 500ml measuring cup. 'How many times can I fill the cup from the bottle?' Ravi calculated: 2 L = 2000 ml, so 2000 ÷ 500 = 4 times!

example.problem: How many 250ml glasses fit in a 2L milk bottle?
example.solution: 2000 ml ÷ 250 ml = 8 glasses

points.label: Tip
points.text: Convert to the same unit before dividing

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 liters fills eight 250ml glasses.

image.alt: Converting and Comparing Capacities — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Weighing Different Objects
slides.storyContext: In the kitchen, Anaya and Ravi weighed various items. A lemon: 50g. An apple: 150g. A watermelon: 3 kg. A handful of lentils: 25g. They realized weights vary greatly depending on the item.
slides.inSimpleWords: Different objects have very different weights.

image.alt: Weighing Different Objects — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Your Kitchen Math Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother has a 5-kilogram bag of sugar. She uses 250 grams for one cake. How many cakes can she make? (Hint: Convert to the same unit first!)
slides.inSimpleWords: How many 250g cakes fit in 5 kilograms?

image.alt: Your Kitchen Math Challenge — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Weight and Capacity in Daily Life
slides.storyContext: Ravi noted what they used weight and capacity for: measuring milk for tea (capacity), weighing rice for lunch (weight), checking if the baby gained weight (weight), and filling a water bottle for school (capacity).

example.problem: Mom needs 500g flour and 250ml milk for a recipe. Has she enough from 1kg flour and 1L milk?

slides.inSimpleWords: Weight and capacity help in cooking and shopping.

image.alt: Weight and Capacity in Daily Life — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Relationship Between Weight and Capacity
slides.storyContext: Anaya discovered something interesting: 1 liter of water weighs 1 kilogram! 'So 500ml of water weighs 500 grams!' she exclaimed. This only works for water; oil and honey weigh differently.

points.label: Other Liquids
points.text: May have different weights per volume

slides.inSimpleWords: One liter of water weighs one kilogram.

image.alt: Relationship Between Weight and Capacity — Weight and Capacity

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Measurement Mastery
slides.storyContext: They learned that weight measures heaviness in grams and kilograms, capacity measures volume in milliliters and liters, and both are essential for cooking and daily life.

points.label: Conversions
points.text: Convert to same unit before comparing

slides.inSimpleWords: Weight and capacity measure how heavy and how full.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Measurement Mastery — Weight and Capacity

subject: The World Around Us
title: Anaya and Ravi Trace the River's Path
hook: Two friends follow a river from mountain springs to the sea.

slides.title: Following the Water
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi visited a mountain village. At the highest peak, they found a small spring of water trickling down. 'This tiny stream starts the river!' Anaya exclaimed. They decided to follow it all the way down.

points.label: Source
points.text: River begins in mountains as springs or melting snow

slides.inSimpleWords: Rivers start high in mountains as tiny springs.

image.alt: Following the Water — Journey of a River

slides.title: The Upper Course: Youth of the River
slides.storyContext: As they walked downhill, the stream grew faster and more powerful. 'The water rushes down steeply!' said Ravi. They saw it carving V-shaped valleys and creating small waterfalls. Anaya noted: 'This is the river's youth—young, fast, and active.'

points.label: Tributaries
points.text: Small streams join the main river

slides.inSimpleWords: Young rivers flow fast downhill in steep valleys.

image.alt: The Upper Course: Youth of the River — Journey of a River

slides.title: Erosion in the Upper Course
slides.storyContext: Ravi picked up a smooth pebble from the river. 'It's worn smooth!' he said. Anaya explained: 'Fast water carries rocks and boulders, grinding them smaller over years. Eventually they become sand.'

example.problem: Why do river rocks become smooth over time?
example.solution: Fast flowing water constantly tumbles and grinds rocks against each other, wearing them smooth.

points.label: Erosion
points.text: Water shapes the land by wearing it down

slides.inSimpleWords: Rushing water smooths and shapes river rocks.

image.alt: Erosion in the Upper Course — Journey of a River

slides.title: The Middle Course: Adult River
slides.storyContext: Days later, Anaya and Ravi reached flatter land. The river had become wider and slower. 'Now it's like an adult—still strong but more relaxed,' observed Anaya. They saw meanders (curves) and oxbow lakes. Ravi noticed the river deposited mud on its banks.

points.label: Middle Course
points.text: River widens, flow slows, many curves (meanders)

points.label: Oxbow Lake
points.text: Loop of river cut off from main channel

slides.inSimpleWords: Adult rivers flow slower and curve across flat lands.

image.alt: The Middle Course: Adult River — Journey of a River

slides.title: Meanders and Oxbow Lakes
slides.storyContext: Anaya drew a map of the winding river. 'See how it curves back and forth? Those S-curves are meanders. Sometimes they loop so much, the river cuts the loop off, leaving an oxbow lake!'

example.problem: How does an oxbow lake form?
example.solution: A meander curves so much it loops back and nearly touches itself. The river cuts through the narrow neck, leaving a curved lake.

points.label: Process
points.text: Takes years of erosion and deposition to form

slides.inSimpleWords: Curved river loops sometimes separate into oxbow lakes.

image.alt: Meanders and Oxbow Lakes — Journey of a River

slides.title: The Lower Course: Mouth and Delta
slides.storyContext: Finally, Anaya and Ravi reached the plains where the river met the sea. 'The water is almost still! The gradient (slope) is so gentle,' noted Anaya. They saw a delta—a fan-shaped area where the river splits into many channels, dropping sediment and forming islands.

points.label: Lower Course
points.text: River widens greatly, flows very slowly

points.label: Delta
points.text: Fan-shaped area where river meets sea

points.label: Mouth
points.text: Opening where river enters the ocean

slides.inSimpleWords: Old rivers reach flat land, split into channels, meet sea.

image.alt: The Lower Course: Mouth and Delta — Journey of a River

slides.title: The Nile Delta and Other Famous Deltas
slides.storyContext: Anaya read about the Nile Delta in Egypt and the Sundarbans delta in Bengal. 'These are perfect fans of fertile land where rivers split before meeting the sea. Farmers use this rich soil!', she explained to Ravi.

example.problem: Why are river deltas good for farming?
example.solution: Deltas have rich sediment deposited by the river, making soil very fertile for crops.

points.label: Fertile Soil
points.text: Sediment creates nutritious land for agriculture

slides.inSimpleWords: Deltas have rich soil perfect for farming.

image.alt: The Nile Delta and Other Famous Deltas — Journey of a River

slides.title: Your River Journey Challenge
slides.storyContext: Imagine a river you know or make up. Describe its journey from source to mouth. What happens to the water's speed? How does the valley shape change? What lives along different parts?

points.label: Think
points.text: Map upper, middle, and lower courses; note changes

slides.inSimpleWords: Trace a river from mountain source to sea.

image.alt: Your River Journey Challenge — Journey of a River

slides.title: Rivers and the Water Cycle
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked: 'Where does all this water come from?' Anaya explained: 'Rain falls on mountains, flows to the sea, then evaporates to clouds, and falls as rain again. Rivers are the water cycle in action!'

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Water from sea and land rises as vapor

points.label: Condensation
points.text: Vapor cools in air and forms clouds

points.label: Precipitation
points.text: Water falls as rain or snow

points.label: Run-off
points.text: Rain flows downhill to rivers and sea

slides.inSimpleWords: Rivers carry water in the endless water cycle.

image.alt: Rivers and the Water Cycle — Journey of a River

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's River Discovery
slides.storyContext: They traced the river's complete journey, learning that rivers shape the land, support life, and connect mountains to seas as part of Earth's water cycle.

points.label: Lower Course
points.text: Slow, very wide, delta at sea

slides.inSimpleWords: Rivers journey from mountains to sea, shaping Earth.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's River Discovery — Journey of a River

subject: The World Around Us
title: Anaya and Ravi's Food Detective Adventure
hook: Two friends uncover where all the food on their plate comes from.

slides.title: Breakfast Mystery
slides.storyContext: Anaya looked at her breakfast plate: rice, eggs, milk, and banana. 'Where did all this come from?' she wondered. Ravi replied, 'Let's find out!' Together they began investigating where each food originated.

points.label: Question
points.text: All food has a source in nature

slides.inSimpleWords: Every food on our plate comes from plants or animals.

image.alt: Breakfast Mystery — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: Plants: The Food Makers
slides.storyContext: At the farmer's market, Anaya met a farmer. 'Plants make food using sunlight!' he explained. 'They use sun, water, and air to make their own food. We eat the plants or eat animals that ate the plants.'

points.label: Photosynthesis
points.text: Plants use sunlight to make food

points.label: Producers
points.text: Plants are the first source of all food

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants use sunlight to make food; we eat them.

image.alt: Plants: The Food Makers — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: From Plant to Plate
slides.storyContext: Anaya traced her rice: the farmer plants seeds, sun and rain help the plant grow, he harvests the grain, mills it into rice, and sells it at market. 'All because of the sun's energy!' she realized.

example.problem: How does the sun help rice grow and reach our plate?
example.solution: Sun provides energy for the plant to grow. The plant stores this energy in the grain (rice) that we eat.

points.label: Sun Power
points.text: All food energy starts with the sun

slides.inSimpleWords: Sun energy grows rice; farmers harvest and sell it.

image.alt: From Plant to Plate — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: Animals: Food Eaters
slides.storyContext: Ravi explored the farm. 'Cows eat grass, chickens eat grain, and fish eat algae,' he noted. 'Every animal eats something else to get energy.' Anaya added: 'Herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat meat, and omnivores eat both!'

points.label: Omnivores
points.text: Eat both plants and meat (humans, bears)

slides.inSimpleWords: Animals eat plants or other animals for energy.

image.alt: Animals: Food Eaters — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: Food Chains
slides.storyContext: Anaya drew a chain: Grass → Rabbit → Fox. 'The grass gets energy from sun. Rabbit eats grass. Fox eats rabbit. Each link is a food chain!' Ravi added: 'If we eat chicken, we're in the chain too: Grain → Chicken → Us!'

example.problem: Trace the food chain: Sun energy → Corn → Chicken → Human
example.solution: Sun grows corn. Chicken eats corn. We eat chicken. Energy moves through each step.

slides.inSimpleWords: Food chains show how energy moves from sun to us.

image.alt: Food Chains — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: Food Webs: Complex Connections
slides.storyContext: Ravi asked: 'Can an animal eat many different foods?' Anaya nodded. 'Yes! A fox eats rabbits AND birds AND mice. A human eats rice AND vegetables AND meat. This creates food webs, not just chains!'

points.label: Balance
points.text: All organisms depend on each other

slides.inSimpleWords: Food webs show many animals eating many foods.

image.alt: Food Webs: Complex Connections — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: A Simple Food Web
slides.storyContext: In a pond: Plants → Fish, Insects → Frog → Water bird. But Fish also eat insects, and birds eat fish. 'It's a web!' Anaya drew lines connecting all the creatures, showing that each organism has multiple food sources.

example.problem: In a forest: Grass → Rabbit, Deer → Lion, Eagle. Which organism would suffer most if all grass disappeared?
example.solution: Rabbit and Deer would suffer most. Lion and Eagle would then starve because their prey would disappear.

points.label: Impact
points.text: Removing one organism affects the whole web

slides.inSimpleWords: Removing one species disrupts the entire food web.

image.alt: A Simple Food Web — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: Your Food Detective Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya challenges you: Draw a food web for your area (forest, farm, or coast). Include at least 6 organisms and show how energy flows between them using arrows.

points.label: Think
points.text: Start with sun, add plants, add herbivores, add carnivores

slides.inSimpleWords: Create a food web showing energy connections.

image.alt: Your Food Detective Challenge — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: Food and Nutrition
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother explained nutrition while cooking. 'Different foods give different nutrients: rice and bread give energy, milk and eggs give protein to build muscles, fruits and vegetables give vitamins to stay healthy.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Different foods give energy, growth, and health.

image.alt: Food and Nutrition — The Mystery of Food

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Food Mystery Solved
slides.storyContext: They discovered that all food starts with the sun, plants make food, animals eat to survive, and everything connects in food chains and webs. Every meal is a story of nature's connections.

points.label: Producers
points.text: Plants make food from sun energy

points.label: Consumers
points.text: Animals eat plants or other animals

slides.inSimpleWords: Food mysteries reveal nature's connected networks.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Food Mystery Solved — The Mystery of Food

subject: The World Around Us
title: Anaya and Ravi's Energy Experiment
hook: Two friends discover energy in motion, heat, and light all around them.

slides.title: The Bouncing Ball
slides.storyContext: Ravi threw a ball down hard. It bounced back high. 'Where does the energy to bounce come from?' he asked. Anaya smiled: 'Energy is everywhere! Let me show you different types.'

points.label: Energy
points.text: Ability to do work and make things happen

slides.inSimpleWords: Energy makes things move, heat, and light up.

image.alt: The Bouncing Ball — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy
slides.storyContext: Anaya placed the ball on a high shelf. 'Sitting here, it has potential energy—ready to move!' When Ravi released it, it fell. 'Now it has kinetic energy—it's moving!' As it bounced, the energy switched back and forth.

points.label: Conversion
points.text: Potential can become kinetic and vice versa

slides.inSimpleWords: Potential energy stores power; kinetic uses it in motion.

image.alt: Kinetic and Potential Energy — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Energy in a Swing
slides.storyContext: At the park, Anaya observed children on a swing. 'At the highest point, the child has maximum potential energy—no speed. At the lowest point, maximum kinetic energy—fastest speed!' Ravi added: 'The energy switches places constantly!'

example.problem: Where does a swing have the most kinetic energy?
example.solution: At the lowest point of the swing, where it moves fastest.

points.label: Remember
points.text: High point = potential; Low point = kinetic

slides.inSimpleWords: Swings show energy switching from still to moving.

image.alt: Energy in a Swing — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Types of Energy
slides.storyContext: Anaya made a list in her notebook: Thermal energy (heat from fire), Light energy (sun and bulbs), Sound energy (music and voices), Electrical energy (batteries and outlets), Chemical energy (food and fuel), and Mechanical energy (motion).
slides.inSimpleWords: Energy appears as heat, light, sound, electricity, chemicals.

image.alt: Types of Energy — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Energy Transformations
slides.storyContext: Ravi lit a candle. 'Chemical energy in the wax becomes thermal energy (heat) and light energy (flame)!' Anaya added: 'A microwave changes electrical energy to thermal energy. A solar panel changes light energy to electrical energy!'

example.problem: A bicycle lamp powered by pedaling—what energies are involved?
example.solution: Mechanical energy (leg movement) becomes electrical energy (generator) becomes light energy (bulb).

points.label: Transformation
points.text: Energy changes from one type to another

slides.inSimpleWords: Energy constantly transforms from one type to another.

image.alt: Energy Transformations — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Energy Sources and Power
slides.storyContext: Anaya explained: 'Renewable energy comes from sun, wind, water—they never run out. Non-renewable energy from coal and petrol will end.' Ravi asked: 'What's power?' She smiled: 'Power is how fast you use energy.'

points.label: Power
points.text: Speed of using energy (measured in Watts)

slides.inSimpleWords: Some energy sources last forever, others will end.

image.alt: Energy Sources and Power — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Simple Machines Use Energy
slides.storyContext: Ravi used a lever to lift a heavy rock. 'This uses mechanical energy to make work easier,' Anaya noted. They also tried a pulley and an inclined plane. 'Machines don't create energy, they just help us use it better!'

example.problem: Why does a lever make lifting easier?
example.solution: A lever multiplies force, letting us lift heavier loads with less effort. Energy is still needed, just distributed differently.

points.label: Machines
points.text: Help us use energy more efficiently

slides.inSimpleWords: Levers and pulleys help us use energy wisely.

image.alt: Simple Machines Use Energy — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Your Energy Detective Challenge
slides.storyContext: Find 5 things at home that use energy. For each, identify: What energy type it uses, Where it comes from, How it's transformed, and Whether it's renewable.

points.label: Think
points.text: Lightbulb, fan, heater, phone, refrigerator—all use different energies

slides.inSimpleWords: Explore how things around you use different energies.

image.alt: Your Energy Detective Challenge — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Energy Conservation and Efficiency
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father showed her LED bulbs using less electricity than old bulbs. 'We conserve energy by using it wisely,' he said. Ravi added: 'Riding a bicycle instead of a car saves energy, and growing food locally uses less energy in transport!'

points.label: Efficiency
points.text: Getting more work from same energy

slides.inSimpleWords: Using energy wisely helps save resources for future.

image.alt: Energy Conservation and Efficiency — Energy - How Things Work

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Energy Mastery
slides.storyContext: They learned that energy powers everything, transforms constantly, comes from many sources, and must be used wisely to protect our planet.

points.label: Responsibility
points.text: Use energy wisely for a sustainable future

slides.inSimpleWords: Energy powers our world; use it wisely.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Energy Mastery — Energy - How Things Work

subject: The World Around Us
title: Anaya and Ravi's Water Quest
hook: Two friends explore water's incredible properties and vital role in life.

slides.title: The Importance of Water
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi visited a village suffering from drought. 'Without water, plants die, animals leave, and people struggle,' Ravi observed sadly. An old farmer said: 'Water is life itself.' The children decided to understand water better.

points.label: Fact
points.text: Water is essential for all life on Earth

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is the most important resource for living things.

image.alt: The Importance of Water — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Properties of Water
slides.storyContext: In a school lab, Anaya and Ravi observed water carefully. 'It has no color, no smell, and no taste,' noted Anaya. 'It flows easily and takes the shape of its container,' added Ravi. 'And it exists as solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (vapor)!'

points.label: Tasteless & Odorless
points.text: Pure water has no flavor or smell

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is clear, flows easily, and exists as solid, liquid, gas.

image.alt: Properties of Water — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Water's Three States
slides.storyContext: Anaya demonstrated: She heated water and collected the steam (gas). She cooled the steam and it became water again (liquid). She froze water to make ice (solid). 'The same substance—three different forms!' she explained.

example.problem: What happens to ice when heated?
example.solution: Ice (solid) melts into water (liquid) at 0°C. Further heating turns water into steam (gas) at 100°C.

points.label: Phase Change
points.text: Heating and cooling cause state changes

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat turns ice to water to steam; cooling reverses it.

image.alt: Water's Three States — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Water on Earth
slides.storyContext: Ravi studied a globe. 'The world is mostly blue—that's water!' Anaya calculated: '97% is salty seawater. Only 3% is fresh water, and most of that is frozen in ice caps. Very little is drinkable!'

points.label: Freshwater
points.text: 3% of water; mostly in ice caps

points.label: Usable Water
points.text: Only about 1% is available for humans

slides.inSimpleWords: 97% of Earth's water is salty; only 3% is fresh.

image.alt: Water on Earth — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: The Water Cycle in Action
slides.storyContext: Anaya created a water cycle model: Water from a cup under sunlight evaporated (became vapor), condensed on a plastic sheet (became droplets), and 'rained' back into a container below. 'This happens everywhere on Earth constantly!'

example.problem: Trace water's journey in the water cycle.
example.solution: Evaporation (sun heats water → vapor) → Condensation (vapor cools → clouds) → Precipitation (rain/snow falls) → Run-off (flows to rivers/sea) → Cycle repeats

points.label: Continuous
points.text: The cycle runs eternally, cleaning and moving water

slides.inSimpleWords: Water evaporates, condenses, falls as rain, and repeats.

image.alt: The Water Cycle in Action — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Water Uses and Needs
slides.storyContext: Anaya listed water uses: drinking, cooking, washing, farming, industry, and recreation. 'A person needs about 2 liters daily to drink, but farms use thousands of liters to grow food!' Ravi noted: 'Every activity depends on water.'

points.label: Agriculture
points.text: Crops need huge amounts for growth

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is essential for drinking, farming, and industry.

image.alt: Water Uses and Needs — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Hidden Water in Food
slides.storyContext: Anaya researched: Growing 1 kg of rice needs 3000 liters of water! A glass of milk needs 200 liters. 'When we eat, we're using water from around the world,' Ravi realized. 'Every bite is connected to water use.'

example.problem: Why do we say meat requires more water than vegetables?
example.solution: Livestock eat plant feed that requires water to grow. Cows eating feed use more water than eating the feed directly.

points.label: Virtual Water
points.text: Hidden water used to produce goods we consume

slides.inSimpleWords: Food production uses enormous amounts of water.

image.alt: Hidden Water in Food — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Your Water Conservation Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi challenge you: For one day, track how much water you use (estimate: 1 minute shower = 10L, 1 glass = 250ml). Then identify 3 ways to reduce your water footprint.

points.label: Think
points.text: Shorter showers, turning off taps, fixing leaks

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure and reduce your daily water use wisely.

image.alt: Your Water Conservation Challenge — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Water Quality and Pollution
slides.storyContext: Ravi saw a polluted river. 'Plastic waste, chemicals, and sewage harm water and living things!' Anaya explained: 'Polluted water causes disease in humans. We must protect water sources and treat wastewater before releasing it.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Pollution harms water; we must protect and clean it.

image.alt: Water Quality and Pollution — Water - The Essence of Life

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Water Revelation
slides.storyContext: They learned that water is precious, mysterious, and vital. Understanding its properties, cycles, and uses inspires responsibility to protect this essence of life for all.

points.label: Properties
points.text: Clear, tasteless, three states (solid, liquid, gas)

points.label: Responsibility
points.text: Conserve, protect, and use water wisely

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is precious; understand and protect it.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Water Revelation — Water - The Essence of Life
